segments.text: If you're going to learn about peptides, one of the most important things you can understand
is testing.
You're going to see the term COA all the time.
COA stands for certificate of analysis.
But here's where a lot of beginners get confused.
Just because a vendor posts a COA does not automatically mean you can trust the product.
The report itself could be legitimate, but you still have to ask an important question.
Who selected the sample that was tested?
If the vendor chooses the vial, sends it to the lab, pays for the test and then posts
the best result, that test may not tell you the full story about everything they're currently
selling.
That's why independent third-party testing matters.
Ideally, the person selecting and submitting the sample is independent from the seller.
That removes some of the incentive to only test a perfect sample.
There are also different types of testing.
Identity testing helps determine whether the compound is actually what it claims to
be.
Purity testing looks at how clean the sample is and how much unwanted material may be
present.
Quantity testing looks at how much of the actual compound is inside the vial.
And depending on the situation, there can also be testing for things like sterility
or endotoxins.
One thing I really want you to remember is this.
Seeing 99% purity does not tell you everything.
A vial could test very high for purity but still contain a different amount than what
the label claims.
When you look at a COA, check the laboratory, test date, sample information, testing method,
purity, quantity and whether the report can actually be verified.
The goal is to stop looking at a COA as just a piece of paper and start understanding
what the results actually mean.
